title: C1021 — Left-hand headlamp connector
introduction:
I read this headlamp reference like an electrical address book: the drawing locates a cavity, and the matching table row describes its circuit. Start with the connector identity, then move between the face drawing and the Cavity column. Read across the whole row so the circuit, color, gauge, function and terminal reference stay together.

The functions distinguish control-module commands, relay connections, fuse-or-circuit-breaker supplies and ground paths. Those labels describe circuit roles; they do not prove that power, a command or a sound ground is present.

This is a reading guide, with unresolved cavity-assignment and count discrepancies noted below. Physical viewing direction, access, probing, test values and replacement methods are outside its scope. Gauge conventions and the Size and Used codes are not defined here, so I keep those entries as reference data without turning them into wire or tool choices. The metadata Pin Count differs from the cavity count shown by the drawing and the pigtail record; the source does not reconcile that difference.

edits.why: I use the printed cavity numbers to navigate between the drawing and the table. As drawn, the lower-numbered column is on the right, the higher-numbered column is on the left, and numbering decreases downward in both. Gray-filled positions correspond to rows without circuit descriptions; outlined positions correspond to rows with circuit descriptions. This visual pattern helps navigation but is not a terminal-condition check. The outline and side projections are housing features; no release function or physical viewing direction is identified.

edits.text: Read the cavity and circuit assignments
edits.why: The Cavity column connects the picture to the circuit record. Circuit Number identifies the circuit, while Function explains its stated role; Color, Gauge and Terminal Part Number belong to that same row. Read fuse-or-circuit-breaker descriptions literally without choosing a protective-device type. A relay is an electrically controlled switch, but its name here does not guarantee a separate plug-in component. Ground descriptions identify the named return location, not a measured result. The repeated cavity entry has different circuit descriptions and blank qualifiers, so neither entry can be selected as the applicable assignment from this sheet alone.

A pigtail is the connector-and-wire repair lead associated with the assembly. I keep Number, Service Part and Engineering Shell distinct: they occupy different identification fields and should not be treated as interchangeable names. The remaining columns describe the listed pigtail, not a prescription for replacing every original wire with its stated gauge. The count discrepancy remains unresolved, and this reference does not teach replacement or splicing.
This table provides a regional Product Id. It adds a lookup reference without establishing a replacement method or showing that every regional application is interchangeable.

originalAuthorHold: Pin Count is 17, but the illustration labels cavities 1–16 and the pigtail table specifies 16 cavities. The supplied evidence does not reconcile these counts.

Cavity 10 is assigned both CLF30, VT-BN, for the left low-beam relay connection and SBB33, RD, for a fuse-33-or-circuit-breaker supply. Both Qualifier cells are blank; whether these are configuration alternatives or an erroneous assignment remains unresolved.

editorialRevision.scope: Complete independent active-agent review of all 49 primary units, three complete source pages and sole figure, and 4 edits. Count and repeated cavity relay/supply assignment ambiguity retained for bounded identification reading only.
